content: Corneal injury refers to damage to the cornea, which is the transparent, crystal-clear tissue covering the front of the eye. The cornea works in conjunction with the eye's lens to focus images onto the retina. Symptoms of Corneal Injury: Extreme sensitivity to light (photophobia). Blurred vision. Reduced visual acuity. Eye pain, which may feel like stinging or burning. A sensation of having a foreign object in the eye (foreign-body sensation). Redness of the eye, often described as bloodshot eyes. Swelling of the eyelids. Excessive tearing or watery eyes. Causes of Corneal Injury: Corneal injuries are common and can result from various factors, including: Chemical irritation caused by fluids entering the eye. Overuse of contact lenses or wearing lenses that do not fit properly. Allergic reactions or sensitivity to contact lens solutions or cosmetics. Scratches or abrasions on the corneal surface. Foreign particles, such as sand or dust, entering the eye. Exposure to sunlight, UV light from sunlamps, reflections from snow or water, or arc welding. Infections that can damage the cornea. Risk Factors: You are at a higher risk of corneal injury if you: Are exposed to prolonged sunlight or artificial ultraviolet light. Wear ill-fitting contact lenses or overuse them. Have very dry eyes. Work in environments with high levels of dust. High-speed particles, such as metal fragments from hammering, can embed in the cornea. In rare cases, these particles may penetrate deeper into the eye. Diagnosis: A thorough eye examination is essential. A healthcare provider may use fluorescein dye to stain the eye's surface and identify damage. Diagnostic tests include: A standard ophthalmic examination. A slit-lamp examination to closely inspect the eye. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact your healthcare provider if the injury does not show significant improvement within two days of treatment. Treatment Options: Individuals experiencing severe eye pain should seek immediate evaluation at an emergency care center or by an ophthalmologist. Treatment for corneal injuries may include: Removal of any foreign material from the eye. Wearing an eye patch or a temporary bandage contact lens. Using prescribed eye drops or ointments. Avoiding contact lens use until the eye has fully healed. Taking pain-relief medications as needed. Corneal abrasions or foreign objects large enough to cause damage may not be visible without magnification or the use of special eye drops that stain the cornea. Abrasions often feel like foreign bodies in the eye. Prognosis: Injuries affecting only the corneal surface typically heal quickly with appropriate treatment, often within two days. However, penetrating corneal injuries are more serious, and the outcome depends on the specific nature of the injury. Possible Complications: Severe corneal injuries may require extensive surgical intervention or a corneal transplant. Prevention: Always wear safety goggles when using hand or power tools, handling chemicals, engaging in high-impact sports, or in any situation where eye injury is a risk. Use sunglasses that block ultraviolet light when exposed to sunlight, even during winter. Exercise caution when using household cleaners, as many contain strong acids, alkalis, or other chemicals. Products like drain and oven cleaners are particularly hazardous and can cause blindness if mishandled.
